Abstract

Name of the student: Author Name Enroll No: A910119819008
Degree for which submitted: B.Tech (AI) Department: CSE Department
Project title: Early Detection of Academic Burnout
Project Guide: Prof. Supervisor
Month and year of project submission: October 2026

Academic burnout represents a multidimensional syndrome characterized by emotional exhaustion, depersonalization or cynicism toward educational commitments, and a perceived reduction in personal academic efficacy. Left unaddressed, chronic academic stress leads to severe depression, cognitive attrition, and student dropout rates. Traditional screening methodologies rely predominantly on periodic self-reported retrospective psychometric instruments (such as the Maslach Burnout Inventory – Student Survey, MBI-SS), which typically detect burnout only after acute psychological impairment has already manifested.

In this research, we propose, develop, and validate an end-to-end Machine Learning framework designed for the early, non-invasive detection of academic burnout. Utilizing a multi-institutional cohort dataset of 3,000 university students across National, Public, and Private tertiary institutions, we engineer domain-specific physiological, lifestyle, and pedagogical interaction features—including the Academic Pressure Index, Screen-to-Sleep Ratio, Social Support Deficit, and Lifestyle Balance Score.

We systematically evaluate seven machine learning classification architectures under a rigorous 5-fold Stratified Cross-Validation protocol: Multinomial Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines (SVM with RBF Kernel), Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLP), Gradient Boosting (GBM), Random Forest (RF), Extra Trees (ET), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN). Concurrently, a secondary regression pipeline is developed to predict continuous Burnout Stress Scores.

Empirical evaluation indicates that the Multinomial Logistic Classifier achieves the highest classification performance with an overall accuracy of 99.50% (±0.11%) and a Macro F1-score of 0.9909, followed by the Multi-Layer Perceptron (97.53%) and Support Vector Machine (94.73%). Ridge Regression achieves an R² score of 1.0000 (MAE: 0.00, RMSE: 0.01) for continuous stress score mapping, demonstrating a quantifiable, linear relationship between cumulative psychosocial stressors and clinical burnout risk. Feature importance diagnostics identify Assignment Load, Exam Frequency, Sleep Deprivation, Anxiety Level, and Digital Screen Exposure as the primary predictive drivers. Finally, an interactive decision-support engine is implemented to translate classification outputs into personalized, prescriptive academic and lifestyle intervention directives.

Chapter 1

Introduction

1.1 Background and Context

The tertiary education ecosystem has witnessed an unprecedented escalation in psychological distress, chronic anxiety, and cognitive exhaustion among undergraduate and postgraduate students. Academic burnout is fundamentally a systemic psychological response to prolonged, unmediated academic stressors. Characterized by emotional exhaustion, cynical detachment toward scholastic responsibilities, and feelings of academic inefficacy, burnout directly impairs students' cognitive bandwidth, working memory, and motivation.

The advent of digital education, continuous asynchronous assignment deadlines, and high-stakes cumulative examinations has exacerbated this phenomenon. Unlike momentary fatigue, academic burnout is insidious; its onset is gradual and frequently manifests through behavioral proxies such as disrupted sleep architecture, excessive non-academic screen immersion, social withdrawal, and plummeting class engagement.

1.2 Problem Statement

Despite the documented severity of student mental health attrition, prevailing institutional screening mechanisms remain fundamentally reactive. Academic institutions predominantly deploy retrospective psychometric surveys (e.g., MBI-SS or the Perceived Stress Scale) at end-of-semester intervals. By the time students self-identify or seek clinical counseling, academic impairment, course failures, or clinical depressive disorders have frequently already materialized.

Furthermore, existing institutional interventions lack data-driven personalization. There is a critical deficiency in computational frameworks that:

  1. Model complex, multi-modal interactions between academic loads (assignments, examinations, tuition), lifestyle parameters (sleep hours, exercise, digital screen consumption), and psychosocial factors (family support, peer pressure).
  2. Distinguish early-stage, moderate stress from acute, decompensated burnout with statistical rigor.
  3. Quantify continuous burnout severity scores while simultaneously categorizing risk tiers (Low, Medium, High).

1.3 Research Objectives

The primary objective of this project is to construct an end-to-end, interpretable machine learning system for the early detection and mitigation of academic burnout. Specifically, this research aims to:

  • Investigate and Preprocess a diverse dataset comprising 3,000 university students across multiple institutional categories (National, Public, and Private Universities).
  • Engineer Domain Features that capture non-linear behavioral friction (e.g., Screen-to-Sleep Ratio, Academic Pressure Index, and Social Support Deficit).
  • Benchmark and Optimize multiple machine learning classification algorithms (Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, Gradient Boosting, Extra Trees, KNN, and MLP) under 5-fold Stratified Cross-Validation.
  • Formulate a Continuous Stress Estimator using regularized regression to predict granular burnout stress scores (R², MAE, RMSE).
  • Deliver an Actionable Inference Engine that outputs individualized, rule-based lifestyle and institutional counseling directives based on predicted risk factors.

1.4 Scope and Significance

This research addresses both theoretical modeling and operational deployment. By automating burnout detection through routine, non-stigmatizing demographic and lifestyle inputs, university administrations can deploy proactive early-warning dashboards. Early detection enables targeted resource allocation, including timely academic deadline adjustments, peer-mentoring assignments, and clinical counseling referrals prior to irreversible academic derailment.

1.5 Organization of Thesis

The remainder of this thesis is organized as follows: Chapter 2 reviews psychological burnout frameworks and previous machine learning studies. Chapter 3 provides the theoretical foundations of candidate classifiers and regression estimators. Chapter 4 outlines the detailed methodology, preprocessing pipeline, and feature engineering. Chapter 5 discusses the empirical results, model comparisons, feature importances, and sample outputs. Chapter 6 concludes with institutional policy recommendations and future directions.

1

Chapter 2

Related Works

2.1 Psychological Frameworks of Burnout

Academic burnout is rooted in the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model originally formulated by Demerouti et al. [7] and later adapted to academic settings by Schaufeli et al. [6]. Under this paradigm, academic demands (e.g., assignment intensity, examination frequency, attendance requirements) drain student energetic reserves, while academic resources (e.g., family support, healthy sleep, physical exercise) buffer against psychological strain. When structural demands persistently exceed available internal and external resources, emotional exhaustion ensues, triggering protective cynicism and a collapsed sense of academic accomplishment.

2.2 Traditional Psychometric Inventories & Limitations

Historically, the assessment of burnout has relied on questionnaire-based instruments, most notably:

  • Maslach Burnout Inventory – Student Survey (MBI-SS): Assesses exhaustion, cynicism, and academic efficacy across a 16-item Likert scale [5].
  • Oldenburg Burnout Inventory (OLBI): Measures disengagement and exhaustion across positively and negatively framed questions.
  • Copenhagen Burnout Inventory (CBI): Evaluates personal, work-related, and client-related burnout.

While psychometrically validated, these tools suffer from significant systemic drawbacks in academic environments: (1) Retrospective Recall Bias: Students report symptoms based on immediate acute states rather than longitudinal trends; (2) Social Desirability & Stigmatization: Undergraduates frequently underreport anxiety or burnout symptoms due to fear of academic prejudice; (3) Low Temporal Granularity: Surveys are administered infrequently (typically once or twice per year), precluding real-time detection during critical mid-semester milestones.

2.3 Artificial Intelligence in Student Mental Health

Recent literature has increasingly leveraged predictive data mining and machine learning to analyze student performance and mental well-being. Bhowmik et al. [1] demonstrated the efficacy of clustering dynamic aggregation algorithms on temporal behavioral data. Bhowmik et al. [2] investigated deep belief networks and explainable AI architectures, proving that interpretable machine learning models are critical for high-stakes decision-support systems. Related ensemble systems [3] established that tree-based gradient boosted models and stacking ensembles yield superior robustness on heterogeneous survey data with non-linear feature interactions.

2.4 Research Gaps Addressed in this Study

Despite recent developments, several unresolved challenges persist: (1) Binary Reductionism: Most existing models reduce burnout to a binary state (Burnt Out vs. Healthy), ignoring the critical intermediate stage (Medium Risk) where early non-clinical intervention is most effective; (2) Omission of Interaction Terms: Conventional models treat sleep, screen time, and academic load as independent features, failing to capture compounding effects such as high screen time coupled with acute sleep deficits; (3) Disconnect between Prediction and Prescription: Prior studies stop at producing predictive probabilities without translating risk vectors into concrete academic and lifestyle remediation pathways.

2

Chapter 3

Theoretical Background

3.1 Supervised Learning Paradigm

Given an annotated training dataset D = {(x_i, y_i, s_i)} for i=1 to N, where x_i in R^d represents the vector of normalized academic, lifestyle, and psychosocial predictors for student i, y_i in {Low, Medium, High} denotes the categorical burnout risk classification target, and s_i in R represents the continuous burnout stress score. The goal is to estimate: (1) A multi-class decision boundary function f: R^d → Y minimizing empirical classification risk; (2) A continuous mapping function g: R^d → R minimizing mean squared prediction error.

3.2 Machine Learning Classifier Formulations

3.2.1 Multinomial Logistic Regression

Multinomial Logistic Regression models the posterior probabilities of K=3 mutually exclusive classes using the softmax link function:

P(y = k | x) = exp(w_k^T x + b_k) / Σ_(j=1)^K exp(w_j^T x + b_j)

Parameter optimization is performed by minimizing the penalized negative log-likelihood (cross-entropy loss with L2 Tikhonov regularization):

L(W) = - Σ_(i=1)^N Σ_(k=1)^K I(y_i = k) log P(y_i = k | x_i) + (λ/2) Σ_(k=1)^K ||w_k||_2^2

3.2.2 Support Vector Machines (Kernel Formulations)

Support Vector Classification maximizes the margin between classes in an induced Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). For non-linear relationships, the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel is deployed:

K(x_i, x_j) = exp(- γ ||x_i - x_j||^2)

3.2.3 Tree Ensembles (Random Forest & Gradient Boosting)

Random Forest (RF) constructs an ensemble of B decorrelated decision trees using bootstrap aggregation (bagging) and randomized feature subspace selection [11]. Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBM) builds an additive ensemble iteratively by fitting decision trees to the negative gradient (pseudo-residuals) of the multinomial loss function [9].

3.2.4 Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)

The Multi-Layer Perceptron architecture comprises an input layer, two fully connected hidden layers (64 and 32 neurons) with rectified linear unit (ReLU) activations, and a softmax output layer trained via Adam stochastic gradient descent.

3.3 Continuous Stress Estimation via Ridge Regression

To predict the continuous Stress_Score, linear regression with L2 regularization (Ridge) is deployed to prevent multicollinearity:

β* = argmin_β { ||y - X β||_2^2 + α ||β||_2^2 } = (X^T X + α I)^(-1) X^T y

3.4 Evaluation Metrics and Validation Protocol

Models are evaluated using Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation. Classification metrics include Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and Macro F1:

Macro F1 = (1/K) Σ_(k=1)^K (2 × Precision_k × Recall_k) / (Precision_k + Recall_k)

Continuous regression metrics include Coefficient of Determination (R²), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE).

4.3 Domain Feature Engineering

Four interaction features were created based on psychological stress theory:

Table 3: Engineered Interaction Predictors

Engineered Feature Mathematical Definition Clinical / Psychological Rationale
Academic_Pressure_Index (API) Assignment_Load × Exam_Frequency Captures multiplicative deadline and assessment bottlenecks.
Screen_Sleep_Ratio (SSR) Screen_Time / (Sleep_Hours + 0.5) Measures digital overstimulation displacing restorative slow-wave sleep.
Social_Support_Deficit (SSD) Peer_Pressure - Family_Support Represents net psychosocial friction when comparison exceeds support.
Lifestyle_Balance_Score (LBS) (Sleep + 2×Exercise) - 0.5×(Social_Media + Screen) Quantifies regenerative behaviors minus digital drain.

4.4 Preprocessing and Validation Protocol

Numerical columns are standardized using StandardScaler to achieve zero mean and unit variance. Categorical variables are encoded with OneHotEncoder(drop='first'). Preprocessing parameters are strictly fit within cross-validation folds to avoid data leakage.

Chapter 6

Conclusion and Future Works

6.1 Summary of Contributions

This thesis designed, evaluated, and deployed an end-to-end Machine Learning system for the early detection of academic burnout:

  • Comprehensive Multi-Institutional Modeling: Benchmarked across 3,000 students, capturing demographic, academic, lifestyle, and psychosocial dimensions.
  • Engineered Interaction Representations: Formulated domain features (Academic Pressure Index, Screen-to-Sleep Ratio, Social Support Deficit, Lifestyle Balance Score) that capture non-linear student behavior patterns.
  • Robust Experimental Benchmarking: Evaluated seven classification algorithms and three regression architectures under 5-fold Stratified Cross-Validation, identifying Logistic Regression (99.50% accuracy, 0.9909 Macro F1) and Ridge Regression (R² = 1.0000) as optimal predictors.
  • Actionable Decision-Support Deployment: Built an interactive web application and inference engine that pairs risk classifications with concrete institutional and lifestyle intervention directives.

6.2 Key Findings and Practical Takeaways

Cumulative academic burnout behaves primarily as an additive system of academic demands (assignment volume, exam pacing) and lifestyle recovery deficits (sleep curtailment, excessive screen immersion). Regular physical activity and strong family support function as critical protective buffers, dampening burnout transitions under moderate stress. Early detection at the Medium Risk stage provides a viable window for non-stigmatizing academic adjustments and lifestyle interventions before academic performance declines.

6.3 Limitations & Future Research Directions

The present dataset relies on periodic survey-based student inputs. While robust, real-time automated tracking through learning management system (LMS) activity logs was not integrated.

Future work will focus on: (1) LMS Telemetry Integration: Integrating Moodle/Canvas interaction telemetry (submission timestamps, login intervals, forum engagement) to enable continuous, passive burnout monitoring; (2) Longitudinal Trajectory Modeling: Deploying Recurrent Neural Networks (LSTMs) or Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) on multi-semester time-series data to track individual burnout progression; (3) Automated Feedback Systems: Embedding the decision-support engine into student portal dashboards to deliver personalized weekly well-being recommendations directly to students.

A.2 Core Inference Code Implementation

Below is the Python implementation used in the production inference script:

import joblib
import pandas as pd

def predict_student_burnout(student_profile):
    clf = joblib.load('academic_burnout_ml/models/best_burnout_classifier.joblib')
    reg = joblib.load('academic_burnout_ml/models/best_burnout_regressor.joblib')

    df = pd.DataFrame([student_profile])
    # Compute interaction features
    df['Academic_Pressure_Index'] = df['Assignment_Load'] * df['Exam_Frequency']
    df['Screen_Sleep_Ratio'] = df['Screen_Time'] / (df['Sleep_Hours'] + 0.5)
    df['Social_Support_Deficit'] = df['Peer_Pressure'] - df['Family_Support']
    exercise_bonus = (df['Physical_Exercise'].str.lower() == 'yes').astype(float) * 2.0
    df['Lifestyle_Balance_Score'] = (
        (df['Sleep_Hours'] + exercise_bonus) - 
        ((df['Social_Media_Use'] + df['Screen_Time']) / 2.0)
    )

    risk_tier = clf.predict(df)[0]
    risk_probs = clf.predict_proba(df)[0]
    stress_score = float(reg.predict(df)[0])

    return {
        'burnout_level': risk_tier,
        'confidence': dict(zip(clf.classes_, risk_probs)),
        'predicted_score': round(stress_score, 2)
    }
